questions.why: Exercisable any time to expiry. An American-style option can be exercised at any time on or before its expiration date. All standardized equity options are American-style. A European-style option can be exercised only at or just before expiration. The style says nothing about where an option trades or how it settles.
questions.lesson_line: The style is about when you can exercise, not where the option trades.

wrong.Exercisable only at expiration: That's European-style, the other exercise style.
wrong.Listed on a US options exchange: The style is about when you can exercise, not where it trades. Most index options, for one, are European-style.
wrong.Settled in cash, not in shares: That's settlement, a separate term. An assigned equity call delivers shares, while index options are generally settled in cash.

questions.simple: Any time up to expiry, because American style is about when you can exercise, not where the option is listed.

questions.q: What does implied volatility mean?
choices: How big a move the market expects
How much the stock has moved lately
The chance the option pays off
questions.answer: How big a move the market expects
questions.why: How big a move the market expects. Implied volatility measures how much the market expects the stock to move, read from the option's price. Historical volatility is different: it measures how much the stock actually moved over a past period.
questions.lesson_line: Implied volatility is the market's forecast of movement. Historical volatility is what already happened.

wrong.The chance the option pays off: Some traders read delta that way. Implied volatility is about the size of expected moves.
wrong.The option's daily time decay: That's theta, the premium's expected loss per day.
wrong.How much the stock has moved lately: That's historical volatility: actual price changes over a past period.

questions.simple: Implied volatility is how big a move the market expects, worked out from what the option costs.

questions.q: Which word is this: buying a put on its own to profit if the stock falls?
questions.why: Long put. You buy puts to profit if the stock falls. The loss is limited to the premium paid. Shorting the stock instead carries unlimited risk. A protective put is bought against stock you already own, as a hedge. A naked put is written, not bought, and wants a steady or rising stock.
questions.lesson_line: A long put is a defined-risk bet on a drop. The premium is your whole risk.

wrong.Protective put: A protective put is bought against stock you own, as a hedge. Here there's no stock.
wrong.Naked put: A naked put is sold, not bought. It profits if the stock holds up.
wrong.Covered call: A covered call writes a call against owned stock. It's not a bet on a drop.

questions.simple: A long put is buying a put alone to bet on a drop. The most you can lose is what you paid.

questions.q: High implied volatility tells you the market expects the stock to go up.
questions.why: False. Implied volatility describes the size of the expected move, not its direction. When bigger moves either way are expected, calls and puts both tend to cost more. A high reading means expensive options, not a bullish market.
questions.lesson_line: High implied volatility means expensive options, not a bullish market.
questions.simple: False, because implied volatility shows how big a move is expected, not which way. When it is high, calls and puts tend to cost more.

deeper.counter: A call buyer and a put buyer on the same stock both pay for high implied volatility. That is the point: the premium prices a big move in either direction. High implied volatility before a report says the market expects a large move, not a rally.

questions.story: The stock trades at $47. You own the 50-strike put.
questions.q: Which word describes your put right now?
questions.why: In the money. A put is in the money when the stock is below the strike. Here $47 is below $50. A call is the reverse: it is in the money only above its strike. At the money means the strike equals the stock price. In the money describes where the stock sits. It does not mean the put has been used.
questions.lesson_line: Puts flip the rule. Below the strike is in the money.

wrong.Out of the money: That would be a 50-strike call with the stock at $47. The put is the opposite.
wrong.At the money: At the money needs the stock right at the $50 strike.
wrong.Exercised: Exercise is something the owner does to use the right to sell. Being in the money doesn't use the put for you.

questions.simple: Your put is in the money because the stock at $47 is below the $50 strike.

deeper.example: Same stock at $47, two contracts. The 50-strike put is in the money, since a put needs the stock below its strike. A 50-strike call is out of the money, since a call needs the stock above its strike. Same strike, same price, opposite answers.

questions.q: The stock is at $95. The 100-strike call trades at $1.20. How much intrinsic value does it have?
questions.why: $0. A call has intrinsic value only when it is in the money, with the stock above the strike. At $95 the 100-strike call is out of the money. So all of its $1.20 premium is time value.
questions.lesson_line: Out of the money, you're paying only for time and the chance of a move.
questions.simple: $0. The stock at $95 is below the 100 strike, so the call is out of the money and all time value.

questions.q: The stock is at $64. The 60-strike call trades at $5.10. How much of that is time value?
questions.why: $1.10. Intrinsic value is the in-the-money part of the premium: $64 minus $60. Time value is any premium above intrinsic value, so $5.10 less the intrinsic value leaves $1.10.
questions.lesson_line: Split every premium: intrinsic value first, then time value.
questions.simple: $1.10. The stock's lead over the 60 strike is intrinsic value, and the rest of the $5.10 is time value.

questions.q: You buy the 60-strike call for $2.50. At expiration, what stock price breaks even, before fees?
questions.why: $62.50. At expiration, a long call breaks even when the stock equals the strike plus the premium paid: $60 plus $2.50. Between $60 and $62.50 the call is in the money, yet the trade still loses money.
questions.lesson_line: A long call needs the stock above strike plus premium to make money at expiration.
questions.simple: $62.50, because a call buyer must earn back the $2.50 paid, so the stock needs to reach the 60 strike plus $2.50.

questions.q: Your call has a delta of 0.40. The stock rises $2, all else equal. About how much does the option gain per share?
questions.why: About $0.80. Delta estimates how much the premium may change for a $1 move in the stock. So 0.40 times $2 is about $0.80 a share. It is only an estimate: delta keeps changing as the stock moves.
questions.lesson_line: Delta gives you a rough dollar move, not an exact one.
questions.simple: About $0.80, because a 0.40 delta moves the option about $0.40 for each $1, and the stock rose $2.

deeper.counter: Delta keeps changing during market hours, so the $0.80 is an estimate, not a promise. It will typically not predict the exact change in the premium.

questions.q: Your option's theta is -0.06. If nothing else changes, about how much does one contract lose in a day?
questions.why: About $6. Theta is the premium's expected decay per day with everything else unchanged, quoted per share. One contract usually covers 100 shares, so 0.06 times 100 is about $6 a day. The minus sign just shows the value is lost.
questions.lesson_line: Theta is quoted per share. Multiply by 100 to see what a quiet day costs you.
questions.simple: About $6, because theta of 0.06 is per share per day, and one contract covers 100 shares.

questions.story: You bought 5 calls last week. They're up and you want out of the trade.
questions.q: Which order action closes them?
questions.why: Sell to close. You bought the calls, so you are long them. A closing sale reduces or ends a long option position. Sell to open would add new short calls instead. Buy to close ends a short option, not a long one. Exercising would buy the stock at the strike and give up any time value left.
questions.lesson_line: Buy to open, sell to close. Sell to open, buy to close.

wrong.Sell to open: That writes new calls and opens a short position. It doesn't close the ones you own.
wrong.Buy to close: That closes a short option. You're long these calls.
wrong.Exercise them: That buys the stock at the strike and throws away any time value left.

questions.simple: You own the calls, so you sell to close, which ends a long option position.

questions.q: Writing a covered call adds to the downside risk of the shares you own.
questions.why: False. A covered call writes a call against shares you own. OIC says that short call does not increase the stock's downside risk.
questions.lesson_line: The short call in a covered call adds no downside risk. The shares carry that risk on their own.
questions.simple: False, because the short call in a covered call adds no downside risk to the shares you own.

questions.story: You'd like to own XYZ, now $52, but at $50. You sell the 50-strike put and keep enough money ready to buy 100 shares.
questions.q: What's this strategy called?
questions.why: Cash-secured put. You write a put and set aside enough cash to buy the stock if assigned. OIC describes it with an at- or out-of-the-money put, and here the 50 strike sits below the $52 price. The goal is to be assigned and buy below today's price. A naked put has no cash set aside.
questions.lesson_line: A cash-secured put fits only a strike you'd accept as your buying price.

wrong.Protective put: A protective put is bought to hedge stock you own. You sold a put.
wrong.Naked put: A naked put has no cash set aside to buy the stock. Yours does.
wrong.Put credit spread: That spread also buys a lower-strike put. You sold one put and bought none.

questions.simple: Selling a put while keeping the money ready to buy the shares is a cash-secured put.

deeper.trap: The trap is picking the strike for the premium alone. OIC says the investor must be comfortable with the strike as a long-term buying price, no matter how low the market goes. If XYZ falls far below $50, you still buy at $50.

questions.q: What is a protective put?
choices: A put bought to hedge your shares
A put sold to collect the premium
A call sold against shares you own
A put bought to bet the stock drops
questions.answer: A put bought to hedge your shares
questions.why: A put bought to hedge your shares. You add a long put to stock you already own. The strike sets a floor price you can sell at, however far the stock falls. Bought at the same time as the stock, it is called a married put. The premium is the cost, like an insurance payment.
questions.lesson_line: A protective put is insurance. You pay the premium and hope you never need it.

wrong.A put sold to collect the premium: That's a short put. Selling a put takes on the duty to buy. It doesn't protect your shares.
wrong.A call sold against shares you own: That's a covered call, a call written against shares you own. It puts no floor under the stock.
wrong.A put bought to bet the stock drops: That's a long put on its own, with no stock to protect.

questions.simple: A put you buy on stock you own. If the price falls, you can still sell at the strike.

questions.story: You own 100 shares bought at $80. They're now $98. You buy the 95-strike put and sell the 105-strike call, same expiry.
questions.q: What is this position called?
questions.why: Collar. A collar writes a call and buys a put, same expiration, against stock you already own. The put strike is your minimum exit price, here $95. The call strike caps your gains, here $105. The call's premium helps pay for the put. A covered call has no put, so it has no floor.
questions.lesson_line: A collar trades the upside past the call for a floor under the stock.

wrong.Covered call: A covered call has no put, so no floor under the stock.
wrong.Long strangle: A long strangle buys both a call and a put. You sold the call.
wrong.Bull call spread: That's two calls, one bought and one sold. You hold stock and a put.

questions.simple: Owning the stock, buying a put below and selling a call above, same expiry, is a collar.

questions.q: What do you call buying one option and writing another, same type and expiry, at a different strike?
questions.why: Vertical spread. It buys one option and writes another of the same type and expiration month at a different strike. A bull call spread is one: two calls, same expiration, different strikes. The other choices fail on that one shared expiration, or on mixing a call with a put.
questions.lesson_line: A vertical spread: same type, same expiration, two strikes.

wrong.Calendar spread: A calendar spread uses two expiration dates. Yours share one.
wrong.Diagonal spread: A diagonal spread uses two expiration dates as well. Yours share one.
wrong.Straddle: A straddle pairs a call with a put. Yours are the same type.

questions.simple: Two options of the same type and date but different strikes, one bought and one sold, make a vertical spread.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.story: Your journal row reads Put Credit Spread. The legs: sell the 45-strike put, buy the 40-strike put, same expiry.
questions.q: What's the textbook name for this trade?
questions.why: Bull put spread. You write the higher-strike put and buy the lower-strike put, same expiry, and collect a credit to open. It generally profits if the stock holds steady or rises. Put Credit Spread is the Journal's label for the same trade. A bear put spread is the reverse: buy the higher put, write the lower, for a debit.
questions.lesson_line: A put credit spread is a bull put spread. Same trade, two names.

wrong.Bear put spread: That buys the higher-strike put and writes the lower one, for a debit. It's the bearish version.
wrong.Protective put: That's a put bought against stock you own. There's no stock here.
wrong.Long strangle: That buys a call and a put. Here you sold one put and bought another.

questions.simple: Bull put spread. You sell the higher put, buy the lower one for a credit, and generally profit if the stock holds or rises.

reasons: rests on the Journal's label (prettyStrategyType), which can change

questions.q: What does debit spread mean?
choices: A spread that costs money to open
A spread that pays you cash to open
A spread using two expiration dates
A spread whose loss has no limit
questions.answer: A spread that costs money to open
questions.why: A spread that costs money to open. A debit spread lowers your account's cash balance when you put it on. A bull call spread and a bear put spread are examples. A credit spread is the reverse: it pays you to open. Debit or credit is about cash at the open, not about dates or the size of the risk.
questions.lesson_line: On a debit spread you pay to open. On a credit spread you're paid to open.

wrong.A spread that pays you cash to open: That's a credit spread. It raises your cash balance when you open it.
wrong.A spread using two expiration dates: That's a calendar or a diagonal. Debit or credit is about cash, not dates.
wrong.A spread whose loss has no limit: Debit or credit is about cash at the open. On a bull call spread, the net premium paid is the max risk.

questions.simple: A debit spread costs you money when you open it, like a bull call spread.

questions.q: What is a long straddle?
choices: Buy a call and a put, same strike
Buy a call and a put, two strikes
Sell a call and a put, same strike
Buy the stock and buy a put
questions.answer: Buy a call and a put, same strike
questions.why: Buy a call and a put, same strike. A long straddle buys both with the same strike and expiration. It should profit if the stock makes a big move up or down. Paying two premiums sets a high bar to break even. Different strikes make it a strangle. Writing both is a short straddle.
questions.lesson_line: A straddle bets on the size of the move, not the direction. You pay two premiums for it.

wrong.Buy a call and a put, two strikes: Different strikes make it a strangle.
wrong.Sell a call and a put, same strike: Writing both is a short straddle.

questions.simple: A long straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike and date, betting on a big move either way.

questions.story: The stock is at $100. You buy the 110-strike call and the 90-strike put, same expiry.
questions.q: What is this position called?
questions.why: Long strangle. You bought an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put with the same expiration. A straddle would use one strike for both. A strangle costs less than a straddle, but it generally needs a bigger move to break even.
questions.lesson_line: Strangles cost less than straddles, but they need a bigger move to pay.

wrong.Long straddle: A straddle uses one strike for both. Yours are at $110 and $90.
wrong.Iron condor: An iron condor sells a call and a put and buys further-out ones. You only bought.
wrong.Collar: A collar needs stock you own, plus a call you sold.

questions.simple: Long strangle, because you bought a call above the stock and a put below it, two strikes, same date.

questions.q: Which word is this: write a near-term option and buy a longer-term one, same type and strike?
questions.why: Calendar spread. It buys a longer-dated option and writes a nearer-dated one of the same type and strike. It is also called a time spread or a horizontal spread. A diagonal changes the strike too. A vertical keeps one expiration and uses two strikes. A butterfly uses three strikes.
questions.lesson_line: Calendars trade time: one strike, two expiration dates.

wrong.Diagonal spread: A diagonal changes the strike too.
wrong.Vertical spread: A vertical keeps one expiration and uses two strikes.

questions.simple: A calendar spread uses one strike and two dates, selling the near one and buying the later one.

questions.q: A diagonal spread uses two options of the same type with different strikes and different expirations.
questions.why: True. A diagonal spread buys one option and writes another of the same type, with different strikes and different expirations. Change only the expiry and it's a calendar spread. Change only the strike and it's a vertical spread.
questions.lesson_line: A diagonal is a calendar and a vertical in one: new strike, new date.
questions.simple: True, because a diagonal changes both the strike and the date, while a calendar changes only the date.

questions.q: An iron condor sold for a credit can be seen as two spreads put together. Which two?
choices: Bear call spread plus bull put spread
Bull call spread plus bull put spread
questions.answer: Bear call spread plus bull put spread
questions.why: Bear call spread plus bull put spread. You sell a call and buy a higher one, and sell a put and buy a lower one. You hope the stock stays in a narrow range. If it stays between the short strikes, all the options expire worthless and you keep the credit. The max loss is the width of the losing side, less the credit.
questions.lesson_line: An iron condor is two credit spreads around the price. It earns if the stock stays in range.

wrong.Bull call spread plus bull put spread: A bull put spread wins if the stock holds or rises. A condor pairs it with a bear call spread instead.
wrong.Long straddle plus long strangle: Those both buy options. An iron condor sells the inside call and put.
wrong.Covered call plus protective put: That's a collar on stock you own. An iron condor uses no stock.

questions.simple: An iron condor is a bear call spread plus a bull put spread. It earns if the stock stays in a range.

questions.q: What makes an iron butterfly different from an iron condor?
choices: It sells a call and put at one strike
It is built only from calls, no puts
It costs a net debit when you open it
Its loss has no limit if the stock runs
questions.answer: It sells a call and put at one strike
questions.why: It sells a call and put at one strike. A short iron butterfly sells a call and a put at a middle strike. It buys a call at an upper strike and a put at a lower strike. An iron condor splits that body into two strikes. Both take in cash up front. The max loss is body to wing, less the credit.
questions.lesson_line: Butterfly: one body strike. Condor: two.

wrong.It is built only from calls, no puts: That's a long call butterfly: one call bought low, two written in the middle, one bought high. The iron version uses calls and puts.
wrong.It costs a net debit when you open it: Debit or credit doesn't separate them. Sold the usual way, both take in cash up front.
wrong.Its loss has no limit if the stock runs: The long call above the body caps that loss. The max loss is body to wing, less the credit.

questions.simple: An iron butterfly sells its call and put at the same strike, while an iron condor sells them at two strikes.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass; key reworded again here

questions.q: A long call butterfly buys one low-strike call, writes two middle-strike calls and buys one high-strike call.
questions.why: True. Buy one call at the lowest strike, write two at the middle strike and buy one at the highest. It generally profits if the stock is at the middle strike at expiration. The most it can lose is the premium paid to open it.
questions.lesson_line: A butterfly bets on a price target, and the most you can lose is what you paid.
questions.simple: True, because a long call butterfly is one, two, one: buy a low call, sell two middle calls, buy a high call.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Calls and puts with over nine months to expiration when listed are called ___.
questions.why: LEAPS. That's the name for long-dated calls and puts with an expiration over nine months away when listed. More time to expiration means more time value, all else equal. So a LEAPS contract tends to carry more time value than a shorter-dated one.
questions.lesson_line: LEAPS buy time, and time costs more premium.
questions.simple: LEAPS are long-dated calls and puts with more than nine months to go when they are first listed.

reasons: a number in a definition (over nine months when listed)

questions.q: What does it mean to roll an option position?
choices: Close it, open a new strike or date
Exercise it early to take the shares
Add more contracts at a lower price
Let it expire, then open a new one
questions.answer: Close it, open a new strike or date
questions.why: Close it, open a new strike or date. Rolling closes an open option and opens a new one at a different strike, a different expiration or both. The two trades happen at the same time. Exercise uses the right, and averaging down adds to the same option. Letting it expire and then buying again is two steps, not one roll.
questions.lesson_line: A roll is two trades at once: a close and a new open.

wrong.Exercise it early to take the shares: Exercise uses the right to buy or sell at the strike. It opens no new option, so it is not a roll.
wrong.Add more contracts at a lower price: That's averaging down: buying more at a lower price to cut your average cost.
wrong.Let it expire, then open a new one: A roll closes the old option and opens the new one at the same time. Waiting for expiry first is two separate steps.

questions.simple: Rolling means you close your option and open a new one at a different strike or date, all at once.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: My iron condor has four options. Each one is a ___ of the trade.
questions.why: Leg. A leg is one side of a position with two or more sides. This iron condor has four: a short call, a long call above it, a short put and a long put below it. Opening one leg first and hoping for a better price on the rest is legging in. OIC calls that the higher-risk way.
questions.lesson_line: Legging in one side at a time is the riskier way to open a spread.
questions.simple: Each option in a spread is one leg, so this iron condor has four legs.

questions.q: What is an option chain?
choices: A list of contracts by strike, expiry
A chart of the option's past prices
A string of rolls on a single position
The route your order takes to market
questions.answer: A list of contracts by strike, expiry
questions.why: A list of contracts by strike and expiry. An option chain lists all the available contracts on one underlying, organized by expiration date and strike price. For each contract it shows data such as the bid, the ask, volume, open interest, implied volatility and the Greeks. It is a table of what is listed now, not a price chart.
questions.lesson_line: Read the chain before you trade: the bid, the ask, the volume and the open interest.

wrong.A chart of the option's past prices: That's a price chart. The chain is a table of the contracts listed now.
wrong.The route your order takes to market: Your order flows from your broker to an exchange. The chain is the quote table you pick from.
wrong.A string of rolls on a single position: Rolling closes one option and opens another. A chain is the list of contracts.

questions.simple: An option chain is the table of all the contracts on one stock, set out by strike and by expiry date.

questions.story: Your journal row reads Call Credit Spread: sell the 60-strike call, buy the 65-strike call, same expiry.
questions.q: Where does this trade do best?
questions.why: Stock stays below $60. A call credit spread is a bear call spread, and it does best if the stock stays below the lower strike. Then both calls expire worthless and you keep the whole credit. The worst case is the stock above the higher strike: the strike width less the credit.
questions.lesson_line: A call credit spread is a bear call spread. It wants the stock under the short strike.

wrong.Stock rallies above $65: Above $65 is the worst case: the strike width less the credit.
wrong.Stock sits right at $65: At $65 the short call is in the money by the full width. That's already the max loss.
wrong.Stock moves far either way: That's what a long straddle wants. This trade wants the stock to stay down.

questions.simple: Below $60, because this is a bear call spread, and if both calls expire worthless you keep the whole credit.

reasons: rests on the Journal's label (prettyStrategyType), which can change

questions.q: Iron condor: sell the 65 call, buy the 70 call, sell the 55 put, buy the 50 put, for a $1.50 credit. Max loss per contract?
questions.why: $350. An iron condor loses on one side at most, since the stock can finish past only one wing. The max loss is that side's strike width less the credit: $70 less $65, minus $1.50, times 100 shares. Both wings here are the same width, so either side gives $350.
questions.lesson_line: Know the max loss before you sell premium. On a condor it's the wing width minus the credit.
questions.simple: $350, because only one side can lose: the call width less the $1.50 credit, times 100 shares.

deeper.trap: Do not add both wings together. At expiration the stock is above the upper call strike or below the lower put strike, never both. So only one side's width counts, less the credit you collected. Know that number before you sell premium.

questions.story: You sell a call on a stock you don't own. You have no other position in it.
questions.q: How does your possible loss behave?
choices: It grows with no cap as the stock rises
It grows with no cap as the stock falls
It stops at the premium you took in
It stops at the strike minus premium
questions.answer: It grows with no cap as the stock rises
questions.why: It grows with no cap as the stock rises. Selling a call on a stock you don't own is a naked, or uncovered, call. OIC says the maximum loss is unlimited, because the stock can keep rising. If assigned, you must deliver shares you don't own. If the stock ends below the strike, the call expires worthless and you keep the premium.
questions.lesson_line: A naked call caps your gain at the premium and leaves your loss open.

wrong.It grows with no cap as the stock falls: A short call loses as the stock rises. If it ends below the strike, the call expires worthless and you keep the premium.
wrong.It stops at the premium you took in: The premium is the most you can make, not the most you can lose.
wrong.It stops at the strike minus premium: That would cap the loss. A naked call's loss has no cap, because the stock can keep rising.

questions.simple: A naked call's loss has no cap, because the stock can keep rising and you must deliver shares.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the premium as the risk. The premium is the most a naked call writer can make. The worst case is a stock that keeps rising, so the loss has no ceiling.

questions.q: If you write a naked put, the most you can lose is the premium you collected.
questions.why: False. The premium is not your limit. The worst case for a naked put is the stock falling to zero. Then you must buy a worthless stock at the strike. OIC calls a put writer's loss potential substantial. Your loss is then the strike less the premium you collected.
questions.lesson_line: Selling a put means agreeing to buy the stock at the strike. Plan for owning it.
questions.simple: False, because if the stock falls to zero you still must buy it at the strike.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling the put writer's risk small because it has a floor. The floor is zero. If the stock collapses, you still buy at the strike, so the loss can be most of what you agreed to pay. A put writer's loss is limited only next to a naked call's.

questions.story: You sold a covered call on 100 shares. The stock rallied through the strike. Now your shares are gone, with cash at the strike in their place.
questions.q: Which word names what happened to you?
questions.why: Assignment. When a buyer exercises, the seller gets a notice called an assignment. OCC hands out assignments at random. For a short equity call, you deliver the shares and receive cash at the strike. Exercise was the holder's move, not yours.
questions.lesson_line: When a holder exercises, a writer is assigned. On a short call, you deliver the shares.

wrong.Exercise: Exercise was the holder's move. What happened to you, the writer, is assignment.
wrong.Expiration: Expiration is just the end date. Your shares moved because a holder exercised.
wrong.Rolling: Rolling is your own trade: close the call and open another. Your shares would still be there.

questions.simple: Assignment is what happens to the writer when a holder exercises, and here your shares were called away.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking you get a say. OCC assigns exercises at random to clearing members. Your broker then passes the notice to a customer who is short that series.

questions.q: If you're short an American-style option, you can be assigned on any trading day before expiration.
questions.why: True. A holder of an American-style option can exercise at any time before expiration. So while your short option is open, you can be assigned on any day equity markets are open. The risk grows as the option goes deeper in the money and as expiration nears. To avoid assignment on a given day, close the short before that day's close.
questions.lesson_line: Short an option and you're on call every trading day. Close it before the bell to avoid assignment that day.
questions.simple: True, because the holder can exercise any trading day, so the writer can be assigned any trading day.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking assignment waits for expiration day. With an American-style option it can come on any trading day. It gets more likely deep in the money and near expiry. Only closing the short before that day's close takes the risk away for that day.

questions.q: You can't get out of a European-style option before its expiration day.
questions.why: False. A European-style option can be exercised only at or just before expiration. That limits exercise, not trading. OIC says you can always close out the position in the market on any day before expiration.
questions.lesson_line: Exercise style limits exercising, not trading. You can always close in the market.
questions.simple: False, because European style only limits when you can exercise, and you can still sell the option in the market any day.

deeper.trap: Do not mix up exercise and trading. Most index options are European-style, so you cannot exercise them early. You can still sell them back in the market any day before expiration. Exercise style limits only exercise.

reasons: European exercise window is worded differently across OIC and FINRA pages (in conflicts)

questions.story: Your call expires today, $0.03 in the money at the close. You gave your broker no instructions.
questions.q: Under OCC's standard procedure, what usually happens?
questions.why: It's exercised for you. At expiration, OCC exercises equity options that are $.01 or more in the money unless the holder tells the broker not to. That is OCC's standard procedure, and your broker may use a different threshold. So give explicit instructions on any expiring option: exercise, or don't.
questions.lesson_line: Never leave an expiring option to chance. Tell your broker: exercise, or don't.

wrong.It expires worthless: That's what usually happens to an out-of-the-money option. Yours is in the money.
wrong.It's sold at the close: A sale takes an order. Under OCC's procedure, a penny in the money means exercise.
wrong.It rolls to next month: Rolling is a trade you choose. Nothing rolls on its own.

questions.simple: It's exercised for you. OCC exercises expiring equity options a penny or more in the money unless you tell your broker not to.

deeper.trap: Exercise by exception is OCC's standard procedure, and your broker may use a different threshold. If the call is exercised, you buy the stock at the strike and end up holding shares. OIC's advice: give your broker explicit instructions to exercise, or not, on any expiring option.

reasons: OCC's $.01 threshold and broker thresholds can change

questions.story: You're short the 50-strike call. At Friday's expiration close, the stock sits at exactly $50.00.
questions.q: Which risk does that leave you with over the weekend?
questions.why: Pin risk. It is the writer's risk that the stock closes exactly at the strike at expiration. You won't know how many of your short calls will be assigned. On Monday you might find an unexpected short stock position. There is no time value left to decay. Buying the short back before the close removes the assignment risk.
questions.lesson_line: When in doubt, close them out. A short option bought back can't be assigned.

wrong.Time decay: There's no time value left to decay at expiration.
wrong.Liquidity risk: Liquidity is about trading easily. The market's closed; the open question is assignment.
wrong.Interest rate risk: That's rho, a pricing input. It doesn't decide whether you're assigned.

questions.simple: This is pin risk, because with the stock right at the strike you can't know if you'll be assigned.

deeper.trap: The trap is assuming an option that ends exactly at the money just expires quietly. The writer can't know whether it will be assigned, or whether a last-second move changed things. A short call can turn into a short stock position you never planned. Some investors put it this way: when in doubt, close them out.

questions.q: Rising open interest in a stock's calls means traders are bullish on it.
questions.why: False. Open interest counts the option contracts still open, long or short. OIC says it indicates neither a bullish nor a bearish outlook. Every open call has a buyer, who may be bullish, and a seller, who may be bearish. Rising open interest means more contracts are open, not that one side is winning.
questions.lesson_line: Open interest counts positions, not opinions.
questions.simple: False, because every open contract has a buyer and a seller, so open interest counts positions, not who is bullish.

deeper.counter: Open interest rises when a buyer and a writer both open. So every added call has a seller as well as a buyer. Rising call open interest grows from sellers as much as from buyers.

questions.story: A call series has open interest of 1,200. Today's only trade: one trader buys 300 to open. The seller was closing 300 calls she owned.
questions.q: What happened to volume and open interest?
choices: No volume; open interest falls to 900
questions.why: Volume 300; open interest stays 1,200. Volume counts the contracts traded in the session, here 300. Open interest changes only with what opens and closes. One side opening and the other closing leaves it unchanged. It rises only when both sides open, and falls only when both sides close.
questions.lesson_line: Volume is today's trading. Open interest only grows when both sides open.

wrong.Volume 300; open interest rises to 1,500: Open interest rises only when both sides open. The seller was closing.
wrong.Volume 600; open interest up to 1,500: Volume counts contracts traded, and 300 changed hands. Open interest didn't rise either.
wrong.No volume; open interest falls to 900: There was a trade, so there's volume. Open interest falls only when both sides close.

questions.simple: Volume is 300 and open interest stays 1,200, because one side opened and the other closed, so the count did not change.

deeper.trap: Big volume does not mean new positions. If every buyer opens while every seller closes, contracts change hands and open interest stays flat. To see whether positions were added, look at open interest, not volume.

questions.story: A friend buys calls the day before earnings. The report is good and the stock opens up 2%. Her calls open lower than she paid.
questions.q: What most likely hurt her calls?
choices: Delta flipped negative on the gap
questions.why: Implied volatility came down. The market sometimes bids up implied volatility before an event like earnings. After the event it often drops sharply. If a call falls while the stock rises, another pricing factor changed. A drop in volatility tends to lower a long call's value whatever the stock does. Here it outweighed the 2% gain.
questions.lesson_line: Before earnings, implied volatility is often bid up. After the report, it often drops sharply.

wrong.Delta flipped negative on the gap: A call's delta stays between 0 and 1. It doesn't turn negative.
wrong.Open interest dropped overnight: Open interest doesn't set the price. It counts open contracts.
wrong.Her calls were assigned overnight: Only writers get assigned. She owns the calls.

questions.simple: Implied volatility came down after the report, and that drop pulled her calls lower even though the stock rose.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a good report means a call profit. Implied volatility can be bid up ahead of the news. It often drops sharply after, especially if the report has less impact than expected. That drop can leave a call down even with the stock up.

reasons: the story showed a buy the day before earnings, which the owner's rule B22 forbids; reframed onto a friend so the member never models it

questions.story: Before earnings, your platform shows an expected move of $8 on a $100 stock.
questions.q: What does that $8 tell you?
choices: The size of move priced in, either way
The stock is expected to rise $8
Your max loss if you hold the stock
questions.answer: The size of move priced in, either way
questions.why: The size of move priced in, either way. It's an estimate of magnitude from option prices, with no direction and no guarantee.
questions.lesson_line: Use the expected move to size your risk into earnings, not to pick a side.

wrong.It will close between $92 and $108: It's not a promise. The stock can move more or less than what's priced in.
wrong.The stock is expected to rise $8: An expected move has no direction. It covers a move up or down.
wrong.Your max loss if you hold the stock: The stock can move past it. The expected move doesn't cap your loss on shares.

questions.q: A 0DTE option is a special contract the exchange lists on the morning it expires.
questions.why: False. 0DTE means zero days to expiration. 0DTE options are simply listed options that have reached their expiration date. OIC says they are rarely listed on the morning of expiration. Every option becomes a 0DTE option on its last day.
questions.lesson_line: Every option is 0DTE on its last day. Time decay tends to speed up near the end.
questions.simple: False, because 0DTE just means an option has reached its last day, and few are listed that same morning.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating 0DTE as a separate product with its own rules. It is the same listed option, on its final day. What changes is the clock: time decay tends to speed up as expiration gets closer.

reasons: listing practice can change (OIC primer dated June 2023)

questions.story: You're scanning calls for a cheap swing trade. The 0.10-delta call costs $0.15 and looks like a bargain.
questions.q: Read as a rough probability, what does that delta suggest?
choices: About a 10% chance it ends in the money
About a 10% chance it expires worthless
About a 15% chance it ends in the money
About a 0.1% chance it ends in the money
questions.answer: About a 10% chance it ends in the money
questions.why: About a 10% chance it ends in the money. Delta is an estimate of how much the premium may change for a $1 move in the stock. Some traders also read it as a rough probability of finishing in the money. OIC pairs a delta under .10 with under a 10% chance of being in the money. Such an option needs a strong move to be worth anything at expiry.
questions.lesson_line: A low-delta option is cheap because it probably won't pay. Price the odds, not the ticket.

wrong.About a 10% chance it expires worthless: That flips it. Read as odds, 0.10 is about a 10% chance of ending in the money. Expiring worthless is the likely result.
wrong.About a 15% chance it ends in the money: That reads the $0.15 price as the odds. The price is the premium. Read as odds, the 0.10 delta gives about 10%.
wrong.About a 0.1% chance it ends in the money: A 0.10 delta read as odds is about 10%, not 0.1%. OIC pairs a delta under .10 with under a 10% chance.

questions.simple: About a 10% chance, because some traders read a 0.10 delta as rough odds of the option ending in the money.

deeper.trap: A $0.15 premium looks small. Read as odds, though, a 0.10 delta call usually finishes out of the money, and then the whole premium is lost. The low price reflects low odds, not a bargain.

reasons: delta as probability is a trader convention, not a definition (in conflicts)

questions.story: You own 100 shares of a leading stock you expect to run for months. A friend says to sell covered calls for income.
questions.q: What's the catch for your plan?
choices: Your upside is capped at the strike
You lose the premium if it falls
questions.answer: Your upside is capped at the strike
questions.why: Your upside is capped at the strike. While the short call is open, you give up much of the stock's profit potential. If the stock rallies past the strike, your shares are likely to be called away. The call adds no downside risk, and you keep the premium either way. The cost is the big move you wanted.
questions.lesson_line: Don't sell calls on a stock you want to hold for the big move.

wrong.Your downside risk becomes unlimited: The short call doesn't add downside risk. The stock's own risk is what it was.
wrong.You must buy 100 more shares: Your 100 shares already cover one call. There's nothing more to buy.
wrong.You lose the premium if it falls: You keep the premium whatever the stock does. The buyer paid it to you.

questions.simple: Selling covered calls caps your upside at the strike, which hurts if you expect a big, long run.

deeper.trap: The trap is the word income. You keep the premium whatever happens, but while the call is open you give up much of the upside. If the stock rallies past the strike, the shares are likely to be called away. That can happen right in the middle of the run you held for.

questions.q: When you buy a call, you can lose more than the premium you paid.
questions.why: False. An option holder cannot lose more than the price paid for the option. The worst case is holding the call to expiration with the stock below the strike. Then the whole premium is gone. The unlimited loss belongs to the call writer, not the buyer.
questions.lesson_line: Buying options caps the loss at the premium. Size that premium as your full risk, because all of it can go.
questions.simple: False, because a call buyer can lose only the premium paid, and no more.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a capped loss is a small one. All of the premium can go if the call ends below the strike at expiration. Size the trade as if the whole premium will be lost.

questions.q: Standard monthly equity options generally have their last trading day on the third Friday of the month.
questions.why: True. For standard equity options, the last trading day is generally the third Friday of the expiration month. If that Friday is an exchange holiday, the last trading day is the Thursday before. Many products also list weekly expirations, so check the exact date on each contract.
questions.lesson_line: Read the expiration date on every contract. Not every option expires on the third Friday.
questions.simple: True, because standard monthly equity options generally stop trading on the third Friday, unless that day is a market holiday.

deeper.trap: Not every option ends on the third Friday. Many products list weekly expirations, and a holiday moves the last trading day to the Thursday before. Read the exact date on each contract you trade.

reasons: expiration schedule is a date rule that can change

questions.story: A setup triggers, and you buy one call instead of the shares. The call costs $2.00.
questions.q: Under our rules, what is your stop on the call?
choices: Sell if the call loses half
Just under the stock's day low
questions.why: The full premium you paid. Our rule: the premium paid is the stop. We trade shares, and options are only a defined-risk alternative. So the whole $2.00 is the risk you plan for.
questions.simple: The full premium, because our rule makes the premium paid on an option the stop.
questions.lesson_line: On an option, the premium paid is the stop. Plan for losing all of it.

wrong.Sell if the call loses half: Our rule adds no cut like that. On an option, the premium paid is the stop.
wrong.Just under the stock's day low: That's our default stop for shares. On an option, the premium paid is the stop.
wrong.About 3% under your entry: On shares, the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. On an option, the premium paid is the stop.

reasons: house rule (sizing_rule.md section 9, A6 and B25)

conflicts: Expiration day: the SEC's options bulletin (updated July 16, 2026) still says the expiration date is 'generally the Saturday after the third Friday'. OIC's current glossary (Expiration Friday) and Options Basics say standard equity options generally have their last trading day, and usually expire, on the third Friday. q66 follows OIC and is phrased as the last trading day; no question uses the SEC's Saturday line.

European-style wording differs: OIC's glossary and FINRA say 'only during a specified period just prior to expiration'; OIC's FAQ: Basics says 'only on its expiration date'; OIC's FAQ: Options Exercise says the last trading day. q20 and q55 say 'only at expiration' / 'at or just before expiration', which all three support, and q55 keys on OIC's line that a European-style position can still be closed in the market any day.

Exercise statistics disagree across OIC's own FAQs ('more than 72%' closed before expiration, 'about 70%' sold to close, 'about 7%' exercised; FINRA also says about 7%). No question keys any percentage; q19's lesson avoids 'most holders sell'.

Exercise by exception: OCC's threshold is $.01 in the money (OIC FAQs), but OIC says 'your firm may have a different threshold', and some brokers act on expiring positions under their own risk rules. q56 asks only what happens 'under OCC's standard procedure' and its why and lesson tell the member to give the broker instructions.

OIC (Rule of 16 takeaways) says an implied-volatility move 'describes magnitude of expected movement, not direction'; Schwab's Market Maker Move page says the figure guarantees no size and no direction. q61 keys only on those shared points and uses the generic phrase 'expected move', not a platform's indicator name.

Questions use the common names (iron condor, iron butterfly) for the credit versions, matching the Journal's labels, and cite the OIC pages for the structure and the max loss.

Journal labels vs textbook names: the Journal's 'Put Credit Spread' and 'Call Credit Spread' are OIC's bull put spread and bear call spread (OIC's own page titles carry both names, and its glossary lists both as credit spreads). q36 and q49 teach that mapping.

Seen and NOT used: OIC's glossary entry on strike price intervals gives old standard increments while saying many stocks are exempt; OIC's FAQ gives an exercise cut-off of 4:30 p.m. CT for exchanges (time-sensitive, broker cut-offs are earlier); FINRA's assignment page says SPX options are 'tied to S&P 500 futures contracts' (SPX options are on the index); OIC's open interest article has a typo in its third example (Trader A's position 'transferred to Trader B' where it means C).
